analysis.one_liner: Requires federal certification, inspections, and quality standards for mammography clinics.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced in the Senate's final weeks of 1990 with a single cosponsor, it died in committee when Congress adjourned.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every facility performing mammograms — hospitals, clinics, radiology practices, doctors' offices, and mobile units — to obtain a federal certificate proving it met safety and accuracy standards. It called for annual inspections, sanctions and fines of up to $10,000 for violations, a public list of facilities cited for fraud or revoked certificates, and a national registry of women's mammogram results. The stated goal was to make sure mammograms were reliable and safely performed.
analysis.who_benefits: Women who get screening mammograms would gain the most: the bill required facilities to use equipment designed for mammography, employ licensed or certified technologists, and have images read only by physicians certified in screening mammography, with annual announced and unannounced inspections and public disclosure of facilities cited for fraud, kickbacks, or revoked certificates [S2][S3]. Patients would also gain a permanent record of their first screening mammogram and a confidential national registry tracking results [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Sets federal quality standards for mammography facilities, including dedicated mammography equipment, trained and licensed or certified technologists, and physician interpreters certified in screening mammography, so images are reliable and accurately read.
Requires annual announced and unannounced inspections of certified facilities by qualified radiological physicists, checking beam quality, radiation dose, and image quality.

Gives the Health and Human Services Secretary enforcement tools: civil money penalties up to $10,000 per violation or per day, suspension or revocation of certificates, injunctions against facilities posing a significant public health hazard, and criminal penalties for intentional violations.

Requires annual public disclosure of facilities convicted of fraud, false billing, or kickbacks, and of facilities whose certificates were suspended, revoked, or limited, with the reasons — letting patients check a facility's record.

analysis.who_pays: Mammography providers — hospital outpatient departments, clinics, radiology practices, physicians' offices, and mobile units — would bear certification and renewal fees, inspection fees for facilities that are not accredited, the cost of dedicated mammography equipment and quality-control programs, and new record-keeping duties, including feeding data to a national Mammography Registry [S2][S3]. Some of those costs would likely be passed on to patients and insurers, and the registry would collect detailed personal health information from women [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Mammography clinics, hospitals, and mobile units

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden falls heavily on providers: certificate fees, fees for inspections of non-accredited facilities, dedicated mammography equipment, quality-control programs, and 7-year inspection records. Small practices and mobile units, which serve rural and underserved areas, would face the same costs as hospitals and some might stop offering mammography.

The bill directs the Secretary to establish a Mammography Registry holding information on women's former mammograms, plus data on age, race, family history, reproductive history, drug history, and other medical conditions — a large store of sensitive personal health information, with only a general direction to establish confidentiality procedures.
Certification would not begin until after December 31, 1992, so any quality gaps would persist for two more years even if the bill had passed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core design is a fairly standard consumer-protection model — certify, inspect, sanction, and publish — and the public benefit of reliable, accurately read mammograms is substantial, since a missed or misread image can mean a cancer caught too late. The real costs are provider compliance expenses that would partly reach patients through prices, reduced access risk for small and mobile providers, and the privacy tradeoff of a national registry of women's health data. On balance the bill offered clear public benefit for a modest, targeted cost, though the registry's data collection was broader than the bill's confidentiality safeguards were.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate in the closing weeks of the 1990 session, got referred to the Labor and Human Resources Committee, and Congress adjourned in early January 1991 with the committee never having acted on it.

narrative.text: Senator Brock Adams introduced the bill on October 19, 1990, joined by Senator Barbara Mikulski; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources the same day.
No further action was ever taken: the bill sat in committee with no markup, no floor vote, and no House action before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mammography providers came out ahead: they never had to obtain federal certificates, pay inspection fees, or meet the bill's equipment and record-keeping mandates. Women getting mammograms gained nothing, because no federal certification or inspection requirement existed as a result of the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mammography providers, who faced no new federal rules

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democratic senators sponsored the bill and no votes were ever taken, so no partisan split on the bill is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Mammography providers (hospitals, clinics, radiology practices, mobile units)
industries.note: The bill would have imposed certification, accreditation, annual inspections, fees, equipment mandates, and sanctions on anyone performing mammograms, with the worst-acting facilities facing public disclosure and up to $10,000-per-day penalties. Those costs are the price of the quality assurance patients would gain, so the industry's cost-avoidance interest ran against the bill's public purpose.

The bill let the Secretary approve private nonprofits to accredit mammography facilities, inspect them, and certify that they met federal standards — making approved accrediting bodies the gatekeepers of certification, with an annual government evaluation of their performance.

Certified facilities would be required to use radiological equipment specifically designed for mammography, creating guaranteed demand for dedicated machines as non-compliant equipment had to be replaced.
